snip.t: Infection risk: TB in miners and health workers, anthrax and brucellosis (animal workers).
Exposure and geography: Travel to endemic malaria zones, freshwater contact (schistosomiasis), unpasteurized milk or animal contact (brucellosis, anthrax), tick exposure, or cave visits.

Skin: *Lesions (ulcers, pustules, necrotic eschars), cellulitis, erythema nodosum?* — Necrotic eschar → cutaneous anthrax; cellulitis → Staphylococcus/Streptococcus; erythema nodosum → TB or sarcoidosis.
(This statement leads into the next question about anthrax's virulence factors — see Q32 below.)

qs.q: Inhalation anthrax, historically known as woolsorter's disease, is caused by the inhalation of spores from which bacterium?
qs.e: Woolsorter's disease is pulmonary anthrax caused by inhaling Bacillus anthracis spores from contaminated animal hides or wool. It leads to severe hemorrhagic mediastinitis, septic shock, and a high mortality rate.

qs.q: Which genus of bacteria is explicitly noted for forming endospores that can lead to severe infections like anthrax?
qs.e: Bacillus species, such as Bacillus anthracis, form endospores that can lead to serious infections. Streptococcus species do not typically produce endospores.

qs.q: Woolsorter's disease applies to which form of anthrax?
qs.e: Woolsorter's disease is an older term for inhalational anthrax, historically associated with workers who processed wool contaminated with Bacillus anthracis spores.

qs.e: Inhalational anthrax has a variable incubation period that can extend to 6 weeks or more, depending on spore dose and host factors. Most cases occur within 1-7 days.

qs.q: Woolsorter's disease applies to the inhalation form of anthrax.
qs.e: Woolsorter's disease is a historical term referring to the most severe and often fatal form of anthrax, which is caused by the inhalation of Bacillus anthracis spores, typically encountered by workers handling wool or hides.

qs.q: Woolsorter's disease applies to the form of anthrax that affects which organ system?
qs.e: Woolsorter's disease is another name for inhalation anthrax, which primarily affects the respiratory system and is acquired by inhaling spores from contaminated animal products like wool.

ai.title: Anthrax
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Bacillus anthracis is a spore‑forming rod that causes cutaneous, inhalational and gastrointestinal anthrax. In low‑resource settings diagnosis relies on history, clinical picture and simple microscopy; treatment is prompt antibiotics plus supportive care.

sections.p: Anthrax is a zoonotic disease caused by the gram‑positive, spore‑forming rod Bacillus anthracis. It is uncommon in most urban areas but remains a public health concern in rural East Africa where livestock handling and consumption of unpasteurised milk are common.
b: Endospores survive in soil for decades

sections.p: Bacillus anthracis produces two major virulence factors: a poly‑glutamic acid capsule that prevents phagocytosis and a tripartite exotoxin (protective antigen, lethal factor, edema factor).
Transmission occurs via contact with infected animals or contaminated animal products, inhalation of spores, or ingestion of contaminated food. Spores are the environmental reservoir.

t.b: Detects Gram‑positive rods; positive in cutaneous anthrax
Shows acid‑fast bacilli; useful when microscopy is available

sections.p: Three clinical forms exist: cutaneous (most common), inhalational (most severe) and gastrointestinal. Each has distinct features and prognoses.
b: Cutaneous – painless ulcer with black eschar, regional lymphadenopathy
Inhalational – fever, cough, haemoptysis, rapidly progressive respiratory failure
Gastrointestinal – abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, shock

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, diagnosis is clinical. When available, simple microscopy and culture confirm the organism. Rapid antigen tests are emerging but not widely used.
b: Clinical triad for cutaneous anthrax – painless ulcer, black eschar, lymphadenopathy

t.b: Shows Gram‑positive rods; positive supports diagnosis
Growth of non‑hemolytic colonies after 24‑48h; confirms B. anthracis
Highly sensitive; used when laboratory capacity exists

sections.p: Early antibiotic therapy is lifesaving. First‑line agents are ciprofloxacin or doxycycline; for inhalational anthrax, add clindamycin to inhibit toxin synthesis. Supportive care and wound debridement are essential.

t.b: B. anthracis is universally susceptible to fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and clindamycin; avoid penicillin G due to resistance

sections.p: Remember that cutaneous anthrax presents with a painless ulcer and black eschar; inhalational anthrax mimics severe pneumonia and requires urgent ICU care. In low‑resource settings, a simple Gram stain can be life‑saving.
b: Painless ulcer + black eschar = cutaneous anthrax

sections.p: Cutaneous anthrax can be mistaken for cutaneous leishmaniasis, sporotrichosis or pyoderma. Inhalational anthrax may mimic severe bacterial pneumonia or pulmonary tuberculosis.
b: Cutaneous leishmaniasis – ulcer with raised borders

sections.p: Endospores may not be seen on routine Gram stain if the sample is taken late; a negative culture does not exclude anthrax if the specimen is inadequate.
b: Late sampling – spores may be scarce

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection, provide supportive care and monitor for complications such as shock or ARDS. Vaccination of high‑risk workers is the best preventive strategy.
Any patient with suspected inhalational anthrax or rapidly worsening cutaneous disease should be transferred to a higher‑level facility immediately.

t.a: What is the incubation period for cutaneous anthrax?
t.b: Typically 1–7 days after skin exposure

t.a: Can anthrax be transmitted person to person?
t.b: No, only via spores or animal products

t.a: Is there a vaccine for anthrax?
t.b: Yes, a live attenuated vaccine is used in high‑risk workers
